# Best RV power station + solar combos

The right pick depends on what you run, especially whether you need to run the roof AC. Here are my picks by use case. The links go to the pages where I found each product and its buy links, since I couldn't pull direct product pages.

## Quick sizing
- Add up watts × hours. A fridge at ~150W for 10 hours is about 1,500Wh ([Acquired Sense](https://www.acquiredsense.com/reviews/power-stations.html)).
- A 13,500 BTU roof AC draws about 1,500W running and spikes past 3,000W at startup ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/)). Only the big units below can start one.
- Check the station's **max solar input**. A big panel array is wasted if the station caps it lower ([GetWattLogic](https://getwattlogic.com/articles/bluetti-vs-jackery-vs-ecoflow-van-life)).

## My picks

**1. Weekends and light boondocking: EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus** (best overall in [Smart Energy Edge's ranking](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/))
- 1,024Wh, 1,800W output, about 28 lb, expandable to 5kWh
- Up to 1,000W solar input (two 500W inputs), so you can add panels later
- Pair it with EcoFlow's folding or rigid panels. A single 200W panel works but charges slowly.

**2. Simple and light: Jackery Explorer 1000 v2** ([source](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/))
- 1,070Wh, 1,500W, 23.8 lb
- Solar input is capped at 400W, so two SolarSaga 200W panels is the most it can use.
- It can't be expanded. Choose it for simplicity, not growth.

**3. Multi-day boondocking: BLUETTI AC200L** ([source](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/))
- 2,048Wh, 2,400W, with a built-in 30A RV outlet and up to 1,200W solar input
- About 62 lb, so it's heavy to move.
- It's the best value in the mid-range. Bluetti generally has the lowest price per Wh but a weaker app and support than the others ([Outdoor Power Stations](https://outdoorpowerstations.com/articles/jackery-vs-ecoflow-vs-bluetti)).

**4. Full-time or running the AC: EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3** ([source](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/))
- 4,096Wh, 4,000W continuous, 8,000W surge, expandable past 12kWh
- It would run a 13,500 BTU AC for roughly 2.3 hours per battery.
- It's heavy (a two-person lift) and the most expensive option. The Jackery Explorer 3000 Pro (3,024Wh, 3,000W) is a simpler alternative for AC.

**5. Big capacity for less money: ALLPOWERS R4000** ([buy here](https://dealectric.com/go/allpowers-r4000-3456wh))
- 3,456Wh, 3,600W at 120V, RV outlet, 2,000W solar input, 5-year warranty, 45 kg
- The store price is $1,499. The page lists code EXTRA12 (12% off orders over $1,200) at about $1,319 through 11/15/2026, though it says checkout has the final word. That page is an affiliate link.
- To use the full 2,000W of solar you need panels on all three inputs, since each tops out at 650W.

## Solar panels
The sources named Jackery SolarSaga 100W/200W panels and the Renogy 200W folding suitcase ([NomadSignal](https://nomadsignal.co/blogs/news/jackery-vs-ecoflow-vs-bluetti-vanlife)). Folding panels are fine for occasional trips. For a permanent RV setup, roof-mounted rigid panels are usually better, but none of the sources covered them.

## Caveats
- Prices come from the articles and differ between sources, so confirm them at checkout.
- The EmergencyEnergy article is written for Ontario, Canada. Its power specs are useful, but its electrical-code notes don't apply in the US.
- Hardwiring a station into your RV's electrical system is best left to an electrician.

If you tell me your RV's loads (especially whether you run the AC), how many nights you stay off-grid, and your budget, I can narrow this to one combo.
